text: If you take one idea from this course into your daily work, make it this one. Group by turns a table of individual events into a table of answers. It is the pandas version of SQL's GROUP BY, and the mental model carries over almost exactly.
Every group by does three things. It splits the rows into groups. It applies a function to each group. And it combines the results into one table. Nothing is computed until you apply something.

Group by status, take the amount column, and sum it. Read it left to right. Shipped orders total seven hundred ninety-five dollars seventy-three in our illustrative data. Swap sum for mean, min, max, median or standard deviation and the same pattern works.

Watch what missing values do. The pending order has no amount. Sum skips it and reports zero, which can look like real data. Mean has nothing to average, so it correctly returns NaN. And size counts rows, so one, while count counts recorded amounts, so zero. Use size for how many orders, and count for how many amounts.

For several metrics at once, use agg with named arguments. Each one is a new name, then the column and the function. This produces a customer summary: order count, total spend, average order, and most recent order date. It is the seed of a feature table you will build again in the machine learning courses.

Agg shrinks the table to one row per group. When you want the group's number back on every original row, use transform. Here each order's share of its customer's total. It is the pandas version of a SQL window function with PARTITION BY.
Group by several columns by passing a list, and chain a sort to find the top groups. Next up: combining tables with merge, join and concat.
